blogPosts.title: How I cut a 200k-row data migration from 15 days to 2
blogPosts.desc: Rollbacks, validation failsafes, and why the slowest part of a migration is rarely the data transfer itself.
blogPosts.content:
The migration was projected to take **15 days**. Two hundred thousand rows, moving into a new schema, on a system people depended on daily. Here's how it became 2 days — and how the API on the other side went from 10-minute responses to under 4 seconds.

## The real bottleneck was never the data

The original pipeline processed rows one at a time, validated each against the live database, and had no recovery path — if row 140,000 failed, you started over. That's not a transfer problem, that's a *trust* problem. Nobody dared run it fast because nobody could afford a failure.

So the first fix wasn't speed. It was safety:

- **Automated rollback** — every batch wrote an undo log before committing. A failure meant reverting one batch, not restarting 15 days of work.
- **Validation failsafes** — schema and integrity checks ran on the batch *before* the write, not after the disaster.

Once failure became cheap, speed became free. Batching + parallel workers did the rest.

## Then the API caught fire

Post-migration, a key endpoint started taking **10 minutes** to respond. Profiling showed the classic culprit: the handler made redundant database queries inside a loop — the new schema had made an old query pattern catastrophically expensive.

The fix was two moves:

```text
1. In-memory caching for the hot, rarely-changing lookups
2. Parallelising the independent queries instead of awaiting them in sequence
```

Response time: **10 minutes → under 4 seconds.**

## What I'd tell past me

> Make failure cheap first. Optimisation without a rollback plan is just gambling at higher speed.

Also: AWS CloudWatch is your friend. Watching the post-migration logs live is how we caught the bottleneck on day one instead of in a user complaint on day ten.

blogPosts.title: The bash pipeline that gives every engineer 2–3 hours back
blogPosts.desc: Five microservices, Docker, Prisma migrations and seed data — collapsed into a single command.
blogPosts.content:
Our HRMS platform runs as **5 microservices**, each with its own database concerns, migrations, and seed data. Setting up a local environment used to be a rite of passage: clone, configure, start containers in the right order, run Prisma migrations per service, seed, debug whatever broke. Estimated cost: **2–3 hours per engineer, per setup.**

## The principle: setup is a product

I treated developer setup like any other backend feature — with a contract, error handling, and idempotency. The result is one bash pipeline that:

- Brings up all Docker services in dependency order
- Waits for health checks (not `sleep 10` and a prayer)
- Runs Prisma migrations across all 5 services
- Seeds consistent test data
- Prints a status table of what's running where

```bash
./dev up        # everything, from zero
./dev migrate   # just the schema work
./dev reset     # nuke and rebuild, idempotently
```

## Small details that mattered

**Health checks over timers.** Waiting on `pg_isready` instead of arbitrary sleeps removed the flakiest failure class entirely.

**Idempotency.** Every step can be re-run safely. Half-finished setups were the biggest time sink — a script you can only run once on a clean machine is a script nobody trusts.

**Loud failures.** When something breaks, the script says *which* service, *which* step, and what to try. Debugging info is part of the interface.

> DX work compounds. One afternoon of scripting, multiplied across every engineer and every fresh setup, pays for itself the first week.
